articles.title_original: Training-Free On-Policy Distillation
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.22236v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: On-policy distillation consolidates specialist models into one student at the price of rollouts, teacher passes and gradient steps for every teacher. We show that the consolidation does not need training: with forward passes only, the capabilities of separately tuned specialists can be aggregated into one model that is, on average, more accurate than either specialist alone. When specialists share a base model, distillation has an exact layer-wise solution: each linear layer of the fused model must reproduce every specialist's output on the inputs that specialist receives while reading its own answers, a least-squares problem whose solution needs only the second moments of those inputs. One forward pass over a few hundred rollouts provides them. We call this training-free on-policy distillation. What the rollouts contain matters more than the solver: answers truncated in repetition loops are few among a mathematics specialist's rollouts but carry a large share of their tokens, and removing them lifts the fused model on AIME25 from task arithmetic's level to the specialist's at matched precision. On Olmo-3-7B, a few GPU-hours of forward computation per specialist yield a generalist that keeps most of each specialist's gain on each of seven mathematics and code benchmarks.

articles.title_original: Batched Contextual Reinforcement II: Does RLVR Need Long Rollout Windows?
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.22887v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Long rollout windows make reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) expensive, yet simply shortening them can remove the correctness signal: when every single-problem rollout truncates before an answer, group-relative accuracy advantages vanish. As a technical continuation of Batched Contextual Reinforcement (BCR), we study how concurrent rewards relax this dependence on long windows. Concurrent Constraint Reinforcement (CCR) places three independently verifiable problems in one capped training completion. Correct answers completed before truncation retain credit, while a shared budget encourages shorter useful reasoning without an explicit length penalty. We connect this mechanism to conditional reward- and update-variance analyses and study 4B and 8B mathematical reasoning models. Against single-problem GRPO with a 32k window, CCR with an 8,000-token window reduces tokens per training step from 975,464 to 174,957 on 4B and from 793,832 to 165,788 on 8B, saving 82.1% and 79.1%, respectively. An 8B training trace shows increasing accuracy reward alongside shorter completions. Single-problem evaluations provide supporting evidence of retained reasoning quality. These results identify reward-preserving training structure as a practical route to lower per-step cost in short-window RLVR.

articles.title_original: Towards Hyperparameter Transfer for Differentially Private Optimization
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.22976v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Scaling laws and hyperparameter tuning remain central challenges in training large-scale models, particularly under differential privacy (DP), where optimization is further complicated by noise injection and per-sample gradient clipping. While Maximal Update Parametrization ($\mu$P) allows for zero-shot hyperparameter transfer in standard training, we show that it fails under DP constraints due to the distinct spectral properties of high-dimensional noise versus low-rank gradients. In this work, we introduce DP-$\mu$P, a theoretically grounded framework that extends $\mu$P to the privacy-preserving setting. By analyzing the interaction between gradient clipping, noise injection, and feature learning, we derive a Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) condition that governs layer-wise learning rate scaling. Combining this with our proposed spectral scaling formulation, we provide specific scaling rules for DP-SGD, DP-Adam, and DP-Muon optimizers. Empirically, we demonstrate that DP-$\mu$P enables effective zero-shot transfer of learning rates across model widths on diverse architectures (MLP, ViT, GPT-2), matching or exceeding the performance of individually tuned baselines while significantly reducing computational costs.

articles.title_original: A Stronger Teacher Within: Strengthening MoE Models via On-Policy Bidirectional Distillation
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.23185v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs, but its outcome-level rewards provide only sparse supervision. On-Policy Distillation offers dense token-level feedback, yet requires a stronger compatible teacher, while on-policy self-distillation relies on hand-designed privileged information. We observe that the MoE architecture itself offers a way to resolve this dilemma, as increasing the activation budget per token exposes latent expert capacity and yields a potentially stronger teacher within the model. However, naive expansion degrades performance because newly co-activated experts are not optimized to work together. We therefore propose MoEvolve, a bidirectional distillation framework following a recovery-then-improvement strategy: we first restore the activation-expanded high-$k$ model and further strengthen it by exploiting its additional active capacity, then reverse the direction of distillation to transfer the enhanced capabilities back into the original low-$k$ configuration, retaining its inference-time activation budget. Across diverse MoE models and benchmarks, MoEvolve improves the initial models by up to $22.2$ domain-average points and outperforms same-budget RLVR baselines by up to $6.5$ points. Notably, the final low-$k$ models often surpass their activation-expanded teachers.

articles.title_original: Response-Informed Value Estimation for Cost-Aware Multi-Turn LLM Routing
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.23239v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Multi-turn LLM routing selects a model at every turn before its response is available, yet task success is revealed only when the interaction ends, leaving each intermediate choice without a label of its own. Logged trajectories, however, retain the response each call produced, which exposes what each turn required and how well the chosen model served it, evidence that outcomes alone hide. We introduce RIVET (Response-Informed Value Estimation for Turn-Level Routing), which exploits this post-call evidence during training while keeping routing strictly pre-call at deployment. RIVET jointly trains two value estimators over a shared state-model representation: a deployable Routing Value Estimator that scores candidate models from pre-call information, and a training-only Response-Informed Value Estimator that additionally observes the realized response. Conditioning on the response turns response-induced return variation from residual noise into an observed covariate, and we show that this reduces the leading asymptotic estimation error of the shared representation. On the MINT benchmark, RIVET solves more held-out tasks than the strongest multi-turn baseline while using 74.7% less total call cost.

articles.title_original: How Data Scales in Agentic Reinforcement Learning: Laws and Synthesis Strategies
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.23946v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Pretraining scaling laws treat training data as a one-dimensional quantity: a token count. Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) inherits this scalar abstraction, but modern synthesis pipelines now generate \textit{tasks}, \textit{environments}, and \textit{trajectories} independently and at very different costs, turning data into a structured design space. This raises a question pretraining never had to answer: given a synthesis budget, \textit{which axis} should be scaled? We address this question end-to-end with three tightly coupled contributions. First, we decompose agentic data into three cardinality axes (task, environment, trajectory), plus a reward-density control variable, and fit per-axis scaling relations on different large language models (LLMs) across math+code, SWE, web, and UI/tool application domains. Across all model sizes, model families, domains, and RL algorithms (PPO and GRPO) we measured, the scaling exponents order as environment $>$ task $>$ trajectory. When environment diversity is decomposed into world and environment-structure diversity, its advantage is mainly driven by the former, while the latter is just comparable to the task diversity. Second, we use the fitted laws as a common ruler to price synthesis methods, capturing each method's efficiency as a per-axis discount factor and identifying critical synthetic-to-real ratios at which collapse begins; these ratios differ by an order of magnitude across axes. Third, we cast budget allocation as a constrained optimization under our laws and discounts, deriving a Chinchilla-style compute-optimal recipe and validating it at held-out scale. The empirical results demonstrate that following the recipe yields up to $1.7\times$ compute efficiency over the dominant ``scale-the-trajectories'' practice.

articles.title_original: Learning Administrative Boundary-Aware Location Encoders via Reverse Geocoding
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.24306v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Location encoders learn compact representations of latitude--longitude coordinates for downstream geospatial prediction tasks. Existing approaches are pretrained using continuous or naturally occurring supervision, such as imagery, climate variables, or species distributions, and therefore do not explicitly capture administrative boundaries or place names, despite their strong influence on many real-world geospatial phenomena. We introduce, to our knowledge, the first method for learning administrative boundary-aware location encoders, using reverse-geocoded text as a self-supervised training signal. Our approach can be applied to existing location encoder architectures and consistently improves their downstream performance. We further introduce RevGeoRQ, a custom architecture tailored to reverse-geocoding supervision, which yields additional gains and exceeds contemporary location encoders on several downstream tasks. Finally, the use of human-interpretable reverse-geocoded strings and residual-quantized semantic IDs provides a more interpretable representation of geographic location than existing approaches. Code and model weights to be released soon.

articles.title_original: DeliMF: Gated Cross-Attention Fusion of Structured Time Series and Clinical Text for Early Intensive Care Delirium Prediction
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.24585v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Delirium affects a large fraction of intensive care unit (ICU) patients and foreshadows longer stays, lasting cognitive decline, and higher mortality. Flagging the patients who will become delirious within the first day of admission would give clinicians a window to intervene. Yet state-of-the-art predictors rely only on the structured electronic health record (EHR) of vital signs, laboratory values, and medications, while overlooking the free-text clinical notes written in the same window, which carry information the numbers cannot encode. To this end, we present DeliMF, a multimodal framework that fuses the structured time series with clinical text. It encodes the structured signals with a temporal Transformer and the time-stamped radiology reports with a clinical text encoder, and fuses the two through a gated cross-attention module. The gate learns a per-patient weight on the text; when a patient has no note the gate closes and DeliMF reduces to its structured-only form, giving robustness to missing text by construction. On an incident-only MIMIC-IV cohort, DeliMF improves significantly over the baselines, particularly on patients who carry clinical text, while losing nothing on those without. Ablation studies confirm the contribution of multimodal fusion and gated cross-attention, and a case study further shows that fusing clinical text with the structured stream recovers delirium cases that the structured data alone misses. We hope DeliMF encourages early ICU prediction to make fuller use of the overlooked clinical text and contributes to the early identification and timely intervention of delirium.

articles.title_original: Process-Aware Event Log Augmentation for Process Prediction under Labeled Data Scarcity
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.24777v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Predictive Process Monitoring (PPM) forecasts future events of ongoing business processes based on event logs. However, deep learning PPM approaches are often limited by labeled data scarcity and the low variability of real-world logs. To address this, we introduce SiamSA-PPM, a self-supervised framework combining Siamese learning with statistically grounded data augmentation. It employs novel transformation methods that leverage control-flow semantics and frequent behavioral patterns to generate realistic, semantically valid trace variants, learning generalizable prefix representations without labeled supervision. Extensive experiments on real-world event logs with a wide range of variability, incorporating exhaustive hyperparameter tuning, demonstrate the value of this process-aware augmentation. Compared to state-of-the-art baselines, SiamSA-PPM achieves competitive or superior predictive performance in both next activity and final outcome prediction tasks. An open source implementation of our method is publicly available under https://github.com/SvStraten/SiamSA-PPM-Extension..

articles.title_original: Polynomial Learning of Positive ReLU Networks under Gaussian Inputs
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.25116v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We study positive, bias-free, one-hidden-layer ReLU networks under standard Gaussian inputs. We obtain algorithms with polynomial sample and real-arithmetic complexity, without separation or conditioning assumptions on the hidden directions. When the conditional label mean is a width-$k$ network with total output weight at most one, the learner achieves squared prediction error $\varepsilon$ with output width at most $k+\min\{k,d\}$ and complexity linear in one plus the residual second moment. For arbitrary labels with bounded second moment, we obtain a positive ReLU network of width $O(k\log(2/\varepsilon))$. Its risk is bounded by the irreducible noise variance plus $Ck^3\log^{9/2}(2k/\varepsilon)$ times the squared distance of the conditional mean to the target class, plus $\varepsilon$. The proofs combine implicit Hermite moments, orthogonal tensor-train compression, and a direction decoder whose probability of returning a direction far from every atom is bounded linearly in the compression and estimation errors. Exact Gaussian localization refines the resulting direction covers. In the agnostic setting, a cone-constrained convex program with a scale-dependent penalty produces a positive network; in the conditional-mean setting, exact sparsification yields the smaller width. We also establish projective direction recovery and confidence amplification with sample complexity proportional to the logarithm of the reciprocal failure probability.

articles.title_original: Truncate or Not? A Scaling Study of Looped Transformers with Truncated Backpropagation
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.26030v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Looped transformers reuse a shared block of layers to increase computational depth without increasing the number of trainable parameters. They are trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT). To save training compute, BPTT is often truncated to the last few loops, but truncation yields biased gradients that may weaken the benefit of looping. In this work, we study the value of truncation in looped transformer training in a systematic way: we jointly vary model size, training tokens, and forward and backward loop counts across nearly 600 training runs and fit a unified scaling law that captures the effects of looping and truncation through effective parameters. Despite the training-compute savings of truncation, our fitted law favors full BPTT when forward and backward loop counts are jointly optimized. In matched-compute runs, full BPTT through fewer loops consistently outperforms truncated settings of the same compute. The law further shows that at fixed model size, the compute-optimal loop count and training-token budget both grow with compute. When model size is also free, the law identifies two fully trained loops as the best looped setting. Experimentally, this setting achieves lower validation loss than the compute-optimal non-looped model with about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and only 8% more training compute.

articles.title_original: A Simple and General Approach to top-$k$ Selection
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.26407v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: This paper considers the Bayesian top-$k$ identification problem, wherein a decision maker is tasked with selecting $k$ items from a pool of items of unknown quality. To assess the items, the decision maker adaptively allocates a fixed sampling budget, where each sample of an item yields a noisy observation of its quality, with the objective of minimizing the expected opportunity cost of the selected set. We propose an approach that allocates each batch of samples by minimizing a surrogate objective derived from an upper bound on the expected opportunity cost. The approach is general: samples can be allocated in batches, the selection size $k$ is arbitrary, and it applies to many sampling distributions. It is also simple and intuitive. We prove that the method's posterior expected opportunity cost decays at an exponential rate of at least half the best rate achievable by any sampling rule. In simulations across a wide range of settings, the method is competitive with, and often improves upon, the best existing algorithm in each setting.

articles.title_original: Rethinking LLM Fine-Tuning via Weight Space Reparameterization: Preserving Safety during Downstream Adaptation
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.26443v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on downstream tasks often weakens their previously aligned safety behavior, creating an inherent trade-off between task adaptation and safety preservation. Existing approaches attempt to mitigate this issue by identifying safety-relevant neurons, layers, or update directions in the original parameter space. However, safety-related information is often distributed across many directions in this space, causing downstream updates to overwrite parameters that encode safety behavior. We propose WSR-Tune, a Weight Space Reparameterization-based fine-tuning framework that preserves safety during downstream adaptation. Our approach constructs a safety-conditioned basis and reparameterizes the weight matrices such that safety-relevant information becomes concentrated in a small subset of directions. We then identify safety-critical directions and freeze them in the reparameterized space, while updating the remaining complementary directions for downstream adaptation. By explicitly structuring the parameter space to disentangle safety and task information, our method reduces interference between objectives and enables simultaneous preservation of safety and improvement in downstream performance. Experimental results show that our method achieves a more favorable trade-off between downstream performance and safety retention, demonstrating its effectiveness for reliable LLM fine-tuning.

articles.title_original: HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.26770v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Harness development plays a crucial role in building capable AI agents. Recent approaches improve harnesses through recursive self-improvement (RSI), but their performance gains often come with higher execution costs. We introduce HarnessPro, a label-free method for evolving harnesses to improve task performance while reducing execution cost. In this setting, candidate harnesses are evaluated using LLM-generated tests without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests. Specialized agents diagnose execution trajectories, plan updates with different performance-cost priorities, and implement them as candidate harnesses. Rather than returning a single harness, HarnessPro uses normalized weighted squared-distance selection to provide cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) harnesses for different deployment budgets. Selected harnesses enter the next iteration, where execution feedback guides further updates. Our experiments cover Terminal-Bench 2, SWE-Bench Pro, and ProgramBench, using GPT-5.5 with Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Across these benchmarks using GPT-5.5 with Codex, the heavy mode of HarnessPro achieves an average pass-rate gain of 2.0 percentage points and an average per-task cost reduction of 26.1% relative to RHO. This advantage also holds when using GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Code is available at https://github.com/pzs19/HarnessPro

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: WeAct: Dynamic Weight Switching as Agent Actions
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.26847v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Long-horizon agents must learn heterogeneous capabilities from interleaved trajectories. Updating shared parameters to learn new capabilities can degrade previously acquired ones, resulting in catastrophic forgetting. As a trajectory unfolds, different stages may require different capabilities, yet conventional joint training and static adapter merging maintain a fixed parameter configuration throughout execution. We introduce WeAct (Weight-level Internal Actions), which trains independent capability-specific LoRA adapters over a frozen backbone and adds adapter selection to the agent's action space. These internal actions use the model's native tool-calling interface for on-demand capability composition in a shared context. Across eight deep-research benchmarks, Qwen3-32B with WeAct improves average accuracy by 6.2% relative to full fine-tuning counterparts despite using less compute, and by 27.5% relative to the strongest static LoRA-merging method. WeAct also supports modular continual adaptation, by adding a new code computation adapter to expand the agent's capabilities and updating the existing writing adapter to improve report quality. Both updates leave the backbone and other adapters unchanged, supporting modular continual adaptation in agents.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: Text-to-Image Generative Modeling Without Language Pretraining
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.26863v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Modern text-to-image (T2I) systems use internet-scale language pretraining for text-conditioned image generation. We ask whether language pretraining is necessary for strong T2I generation. We introduce Halcyon, a family of early-fusion multimodal autoregressive models pretrained entirely from scratch on GPIC, a dataset of 100M image-text pairs. Halcyon-0.52B outperforms LlamaGen-XL/8 (48.0 vs. 63.3 gFD) with 18.2$\times$ less pretraining compute. Further, Halcyon-1.6B outperforms JiT-T2I-XXL/8++ (35.3 vs. 41.0 gFD) with 275$\times$ less pretraining compute. Controlled experiments show that text-only pretraining does not improve T2I generation. Halcyon also learns image captioning by replacing caption dropout with I2T supervision, maintaining competitive T2I generation quality under the same pretraining budget. We show that strong T2I systems can be trained from scratch without internet-scale language pretraining. Code and models are available at https://cs.stanford.edu/~keshik/halcyon

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: Taskonomy: Disentangling Task Transfer Learning
articles.body_original:
arXiv:1804.08328v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Do visual tasks have a relationship, or are they unrelated? For instance, could having surface normals simplify estimating the depth of an image? Intuition answers these questions positively, implying existence of a structure among visual tasks. Knowing this structure has notable values; it is the concept underlying transfer learning and provides a principled way for identifying redundancies across tasks, e.g., to seamlessly reuse supervision among related tasks or solve many tasks in one system without piling up the complexity.
  We proposes a fully computational approach for modeling the structure of space of visual tasks. This is done via finding (first and higher-order) transfer learning dependencies across a dictionary of twenty six 2D, 2.5D, 3D, and semantic tasks in a latent space. The product is a computational taxonomic map for task transfer learning. We study the consequences of this structure, e.g. nontrivial emerged relationships, and exploit them to reduce the demand for labeled data. For example, we show that the total number of labeled datapoints needed for solving a set of 10 tasks can be reduced by roughly 2/3 (compared to training independently) while keeping the performance nearly the same. We provide a set of tools for computing and probing this taxonomical structure including a solver that users can employ to devise efficient supervision policies for their use cases.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: Gibson Env: Real-World Perception for Embodied Agents
articles.body_original:
arXiv:1808.10654v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Developing visual perception models for active agents and sensorimotor control are cumbersome to be done in the physical world, as existing algorithms are too slow to efficiently learn in real-time and robots are fragile and costly. This has given rise to learning-in-simulation which consequently casts a question on whether the results transfer to real-world. In this paper, we are concerned with the problem of developing real-world perception for active agents, propose Gibson Virtual Environment for this purpose, and showcase sample perceptual tasks learned therein. Gibson is based on virtualizing real spaces, rather than using artificially designed ones, and currently includes over 1400 floor spaces from 572 full buildings. The main characteristics of Gibson are: I. being from the real-world and reflecting its semantic complexity, II. having an internal synthesis mechanism, "Goggles", enabling deploying the trained models in real-world without needing further domain adaptation, III. embodiment of agents and making them subject to constraints of physics and space.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: Entropic perspective on AI resilience, data-minimal learning and optimal control
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2310.14421v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Behind the general terms like adversarial attacks and generative adversarial networks (GANs), such criteria as AI resilience and AI robustness gained a crucial importance, in trying to make the emergent AI tools reliable, energy-efficient and safe. From mathematical perspective, these problems boil down to finding a mathematically-sound quantification of the smallest-sufficient amounts of the perturbations of function arguments that lead to the largest possible perturbations of the approximated function values. Here, the entropy-optimising perspective on adversarial algorithms from Artificial Intelligence (AI) is proposed to attack this problem. It is shown that adopting this perspective helps proving computational conditions for the global optimality and uniqueness of adversarial attacks based on cheaply-verifiable mathematical criteria. Further, it is shown how this perspective can be used for developing self-attacking learning algorithms, that generate optimal new data points for training, replacing one of the trained agents with this mathematical criterium. On a broad selection of various synthetic and real-life problems from hydrodynamics and biomedicine, it is shown that such self-attacking learning algorithms allow training orders-of-magnitude simpler and cheaper models with superior performance - and can be used to directly train the optimal controls in complex systems, requiring only a small fraction of the training data and outperforming the as-comprehensive-as-the-author-was-able-to-find set of contemporary AI tools (like boosted Random Forests, deep neural networks, foundational models based on transformer architectures, etc.) in complexity (measured as the model descriptor length) and predictive performance.}

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: Deep learning-based multi-level airway collapse site localization on obstructive sleep apnea patients based on snoring sounds
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2408.16030v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Objective This study evaluated deep learning models, specifically ResNet-50 and Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AST), to identify multi-level upper airway collapses in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) patients using snoring sounds. Methods Snoring recordings from 37 subjects undergoing drug-induced sleep endoscopy (DISE) between 2020 and 2021 were used to train models for two multi-label tasks: identifying obstructions at the Velum (V), Oropharynx (O), Tongue-base (T), and Epiglottis (E) levels, and the retropalatal (RP) vs. retroglossal (RG) levels. Results The AST model significantly outperformed ResNet-50 (P <0.05 after Bonferroni correction), effectively identifying V-, O-, and RP-level obstructions (F1-score: 0.59-0.87, Matthews Correlation Coefficient: 0.50-0.80, and AUC: 0.87-0.97). However, the performance of both models at the T, E, and RG levels remained limited due to small sample sizes, even with the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique. A full-night recording analysis further demonstrated the feasibility of acoustic profiling for airway dynamics. Conclusion The AST models can effectively identify airway obstruction at V, O, and RP levels via snoring sounds. The proposed models offer a promising non-invasive tool for tracking overnight airway dynamics and assisting in clinical treatment planning.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: Help Me Help You: The Aggregate Value of Source and Target Data in Transfer Learning
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2408.16189v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Transfer learning, in regression or classification, concerns problems where one aims to use imperfect data from a source distribution P to improve prediction w.r.t. a target distribution Q. While there is now much theoretical understanding of the unsupervised setting of this problem (where no labeled target data is available), the supervised setting with labeled target data remains under-studied.
  We identify and characterize an interesting dichotomy in the rates achievable in the supervised setting: there is a weak transfer regime where optimal rates are determined by information in either the source or target dataset but not both, and a strong transfer regime where much faster target rates are achievable, accounting for complementary information in source and target data. Furthermore, while previous theoretical tools for the unsupervised setting can be extended to capture the weak transfer regime, we argue that they cannot capture the strong regime due to limitations inherent in the various notions of relatedness they rely on. Instead, we provide an appropriate refinement of relatedness notions---termed weak and strong moduli of transfer---that reveal the two regimes and lead to a nontrivial characterization of which pairs of distributions P and Q adhere to which regime.
  Finally, the above dichotomy reveals a new categorization of existing algorithmic approaches in terms of their optimality or lack-thereof across supervised regimes, and we provide a generic approach that remains nearly optimal in all regimes without prior distributional knowledge.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: LLMs are Brittle to Simple Code Transformations: Introducing CETBench - A Benchmark for Code-Equivalence Checking
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2506.04019v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study how well LLMs can determine whether two programs are functionally equivalent. This is an important problem because benchmarking code equivalence helps assess LLM capability in tasks such as code rewriting and translation. To this end, we introduce CETBench - Code Equivalence with Transformations Benchmark - built from a repository of programs that may solve the same or different tasks. Each dataset instance is created by sampling a program pair and applying a random sequence of predefined code transformations, yielding either equivalent or non-equivalent pairs. Our analysis shows that even simple transformations cause a significant performance drop in state-of-the-art LLMs on code-equivalence checking. These challenges are further amplified in the cross-lingual setting when comparing programs written in different languages. To remedy this, we present a simple fine-tuning-based approach to boost LLM performance on the transformed pairs of programs. Our approach for dataset generation is generic, supporting cross-lingual equivalence checking, the generation of program pairs with varying difficulty levels, and the application of diverse transformations. In our experiments, we perform ablations over the difficulty level of original programs, as well as the kind of transformations used in generating pairs for equivalence checking. Our analysis presents deep insights into the working of LLMs for the task of code-equivalence, and points to the fact that they may still be far from what could be termed as a semantic understanding of the underlying code.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: GenoMAS: Guided Multi-Agent Programming for Scientific Discovery from Genomic Data
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2507.21035v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Gene expression analysis holds the key to many biomedical discoveries, yet extracting insights from raw transcriptomic data remains challenging due to the complexity of multiple large, semi-structured files and the need for extensive domain expertise. Current approaches either rely on inflexible workflows that fail in edge cases or fully autonomous agents that lack the precision required for rigorous scientific inquiry. GenoMAS addresses this by presenting a team of LLM-based agents that integrates structured workflows with autonomous adaptability, orchestrating diverse specialized agents through typed message-passing protocols. At its core lies a guided-planning framework where programming agents decompose task guidelines into Action Units and dynamically choose to advance, revise, bypass, or backtrack, maintaining logical coherence while adapting to the idiosyncrasies of genomic data. On the GenoTEX benchmark, GenoMAS achieves 89.13% CSC for data preprocessing and 60.48% $F_1$ for identifying trait-associated genes, surpassing prior art by 10.61% and 16.85%. Beyond transcriptomics, it outperforms strong agent baselines on ScienceAgentBench and DiscoveryBench, two independent bioinformatics benchmarks. Qualitative analysis shows that GenoMAS identifies gene-phenotype associations that are biologically plausible and corroborated by the literature.

articles.title_original: Bellman Optimality of Average-Reward Robust Markov Decision Processes with a Constant Gain
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2509.14203v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Learning and optimal control under robust Markov decision processes (MDPs) have received increasing attention, yet most existing theory, algorithms, and applications focus on finite-horizon or discounted models. Long-run average-reward formulations, while natural in many operations research and management contexts, remain underexplored. This is primarily because the dynamic programming foundations are technically challenging and only partially understood, with several fundamental questions remaining open. This paper steps toward a general framework for average-reward robust MDPs by analyzing the constant-gain setting. We study the average-reward robust control problem with possible information asymmetries between the controller and an S-rectangular adversary. Our analysis centers on the constant-gain robust Bellman equation, examining both the existence of solutions and their relationship to the optimal average reward. Specifically, we identify when solutions to the robust Bellman equation characterize the optimal average reward and stationary policies, and we provide one-sided weak communication conditions ensuring solutions' existence. These findings expand the dynamic programming theory for average-reward robust MDPs and lay a foundation for robust dynamic decision making under long-run average criteria in operational environments.

articles.title_original: Bayesian Nonparametric Dynamical Clustering of Time Series
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2510.06919v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We present a method that models the evolution of an unbounded number of time series clusters by switching among an unknown number of regimes with linear dynamics. We develop a Bayesian non-parametric approach using a hierarchical Dirichlet process as a prior on the parameters of a Switching Linear Dynamical System and a Gaussian process prior to model the statistical variations in amplitude and temporal alignment within each cluster. By modeling the evolution of time series patterns, the method avoids unnecessary proliferation of clusters in a principled manner. We perform inference by formulating a variational lower bound for off-line and on-line scenarios, enabling efficient learning through optimization. We illustrate the versatility and effectiveness of the approach through several case studies of electrocardiogram analysis using publicly available databases.

articles.title_original: Hierarchical Semantic Tree Anchoring for CLIP-Based Class-Incremental Learning
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2511.15633v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) enables models to learn new classes continually while preserving past knowledge. Recently, vision-language models like CLIP offer transferable features via multimodal pre-training, making them well-suited for CIL. However, real-world visual and linguistic concepts are inherently hierarchical: a textual concept like "dog" subsumes fine-grained categories such as "Labrador" and "Golden Retriever," and each category is associated with corresponding images. Nevertheless, existing CLIP-based CIL methods fail to explicitly capture this inherent hierarchy, leading to feature drift of fine-grained classes during incremental updates and ultimately to catastrophic forgetting. To address this challenge, we propose HASTEN (Hierarchical Semantic Tree Anchoring), a hierarchy-aware framework that uses semantic structure to stabilize CLIP-based CIL. Rather than treating classes as isolated labels, HASTEN leverages external hierarchical knowledge as structured supervision to organize visual and textual features in hyperbolic space, helping maintain parent--child relations as new tasks arrive and mitigating feature drift. Since the shared hyperbolic mapper is updated across tasks, we further stabilize it by constraining its updates to a null space induced by prior-task features, reducing interference with previous mappings while retaining adaptability to new classes. Extensive experiments on nine benchmarks show that HASTEN consistently outperforms existing methods while reducing feature drift and catastrophic forgetting. Code is available at: https://github.com/LAMDA-CL/NeurIPS2026-HASTEN.

articles.title_original: Magneton: Optimizing Energy Efficiency of ML Systems via Differential Energy Debugging
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2512.08365v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The training and deployment of machine learning (ML) models have become extremely energy-intensive. While existing optimization efforts focus primarily on hardware energy efficiency, a significant but overlooked source of inefficiency is software energy waste caused by poor software design. This often includes redundant or poorly designed operations that consume more energy without improving performance. These inefficiencies arise in widely used ML frameworks and applications, yet developers often lack the visibility and tools to detect and diagnose them.
  We propose differential energy debugging, a novel approach that leverages the observation that competing ML systems often implement similar functionality with vastly different energy consumption. Building on this insight, we design and implement Magneton, an energy profiler that compares energy consumption between similar ML systems at the operator level and automatically pinpoints code regions and configuration choices responsible for excessive energy use. Applied to 9 popular ML systems spanning LLM inference, general ML frameworks, and image generation, Magneton detects and diagnoses 16 known cases of software energy inefficiency and further discovers 8 previously unknown cases, 7 of which have been confirmed by developers.

articles.title_original: FLEXI-Haz: Semiparametric Deep Survival Inference Beyond Proportional Hazards
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2512.10570v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Flexible survival prediction does not by itself ensure valid inference for covariate effects or subject-specific survival probabilities. We develop FLEXI-Haz, a semiparametric deep neural network model for right-censored data that combines an interpretable linear component in the log-hazard with a flexible function of time and adjustment covariates. This formulation permits nonproportional nuisance effects while retaining interpretable regression parameters. Under regularity conditions, we establish nuisance convergence rates that are minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors over composite Holder classes, together with root-n-consistent, asymptotically normal, and semiparametrically efficient estimation of the regression parameter. For adjustment covariates with finite support, we derive the explicit influence function for cumulative hazard and construct a cross-fitted one-step estimator yielding asymptotically valid pointwise confidence intervals for subject-specific survival. Simulations demonstrate reduced bias and improved coverage relative to a proportional hazards comparator under time-varying nuisance effects. An analysis of the Rotterdam breast cancer data illustrates the consequences of flexible adjustment for inference on treatment associations.

articles.title_original: The Reward Model Selection Crisis in Personalized Alignment
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2512.23067v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Personalized alignment from preference data has focused primarily on improving personal reward model (RM) accuracy, with the implicit assumption that better preference ranking translates to better personalized behavior. However, in deployment, computational constraints necessitate inference-time adaptation such as reward-guided decoding (RGD) rather than per-user policy fine-tuning. This creates a critical but overlooked requirement: reward models must not only rank preferences accurately but also effectively guide generation. We demonstrate that standard RM accuracy fails catastrophically as a selection criterion for deployment-ready personalized rewards. We introduce policy accuracy; a metric quantifying whether RGD-adapted LLMs correctly discriminate between preferred and dispreferred responses and show that upstream RM accuracy correlates only weakly with downstream policy accuracy (Kendall's tau = 0.08--0.31). More critically, we introduce Pref-LaMP the first personalized alignment benchmark with ground-truth user completions, enabling direct behavioural evaluation. On Pref-LaMP, we expose a complete decoupling between discriminative ranking and generation metrics: methods with 20-point RM accuracy differences produce almost identical output quality, and methods with high ranking accuracy can fail to generate behaviorally aligned responses. These findings reveal that the field has been optimizing for proxy metrics that do not predict deployment performance, and that current personalized alignment methods fail to operationalize preferences into behavioral adaptation under realistic deployment constraints. In contrast, we find simple in-context learning (ICL) to be highly effective - dominating all reward-guided methods for models $\geq$3B parameters, achieving $\sim$3 point ROUGE-1 gains over the best reward method at 7B scale.

articles.title_original: Tensor computing application programming interface: An application-oriented, lightweight API for portable high-performance tensor network computations
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2512.23917v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Tensor networks (TNs) are a central computational tool in quantum science and artificial intelligence. However, the lack of a unified software interface across tensor-computing frameworks severely limits the portability of TN applications, coupling algorithmic development to specific hardware and software back ends. To address this challenge, we introduce the Tensor Computing Application Programming Interface (TCAPI)---an application-oriented, lightweight API designed to enable framework-independent, high-performance TN applications, currently specified for \texttt{C++} and \texttt{Python}. TCAPI provides well-defined type-system conventions that abstract tensor objects, together with a minimal yet expressive set of core functions for essential tensor manipulations and tensor linear-algebra operations, with operation semantics shared across language specifications. Through numerical demonstrations of representative tensor-network applications implemented in \texttt{C++} using TCAPI, we show that code written against TCAPI can be migrated seamlessly across heterogeneous hardware and software platforms while achieving performance comparable to native framework implementations. We further provide open-source implementations of TCAPI based on \textit{Cytnx} and \textit{ITensor} in \texttt{C++}, and on \textit{NumPy} in \texttt{Python}, demonstrating its practicality and ease of integration with existing tensor-computing frameworks.

articles.title_original: Agents-as-Peers: Bias-Controlled LLM Evaluation as Multi-Agent Peer Assessment
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2602.02589v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) evaluation commonly relies on fixed human-authored benchmarks or centralized human/model judges. Fixed benchmarks can age and enter model training corpora, while centralized judges introduce their own scoring preferences.
  We cast LLM evaluation as a multi-agent peer-assessment problem and introduce Agents-as-Peers, a distributed evaluation protocol in which every agent generates tasks, answers the shared task set, and judges the answers of its peers, with no privileged evaluator.
  Self-ratings are excluded from the ranking, and judging is repeated under controlled identity and presentation regimes so that self bias, identity effects, presentation-position sensitivity, and judge severity are measured rather than left implicit.
  In an instantiation with 12 LLMs and 420 agent-generated questions, Agents-as-Peers aggregates 55,440 non-self peer judgments per regime.
  Most agents assign their own answers higher scores than those answers receive from peer judges; visible identity changes scores for some agents; the first fixed answer slot is associated with scores 0.39 points higher than the shuffled baseline; and judges differ markedly in severity.
  On labeled benchmarks, peer scores align strongly with accuracy on TruthfulQA (Pearson r=0.904) and GSM8K (r=0.873). On TruthfulQA, the peer-score correlation is substantially higher than the self-score correlation (r=0.538).
  A benchmark-overlap screen and item-level human audit further characterize the endogenous task set.
  These results support Agents-as-Peers as a cohort-relative measurement protocol whose ranking is reported together with the biases and rater effects that shape it.
  Code and dataset: https://github.com/caura-ai/caura-PeerRank

articles.title_original: Tabular Foundation Models Can Learn Association Rules
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2602.14622v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Association Rule Mining (ARM) is a fundamental task for knowledge discovery in tabular data and is widely used in high-stakes decision-making. Classical ARM methods rely on frequent itemset mining, leading to rule explosion and poor scalability, while recent neural approaches mitigate these issues but suffer from degraded performance in low-data regimes. Tabular foundation models (TFMs), pretrained on diverse tabular data with strong in-context generalization, provide a basis for addressing these limitations. We introduce a model-agnostic association rule learning framework that extracts association rules from any conditional probabilistic model over tabular data, enabling us to leverage TFMs. We then introduce TabProbe, an instantiation of our framework that utilizes TFMs as conditional probability estimators to learn association rules out-of-the-box without frequent itemset mining. We evaluate our approach on tabular datasets of varying sizes based on standard ARM rule quality metrics and downstream classification performance. The results show that TFMs consistently produce concise, high-quality association rules with strong predictive performance and remain robust in low-data settings without task-specific training. Source code is available at https://github.com/DiTEC-project/tabprobe.

articles.title_original: Scalable Posterior Uncertainty for Flexible Density-Based Clustering
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2603.03188v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Density-based clustering is a well-established framework that defines clusters through topological or geometric features of the data-generating density, yielding flexible procedures that have proven effective on large and complex datasets. We address the problem of obtaining scalable Bayesian-style uncertainty quantification by combining density-based clustering with martingale posterior distributions. Density uncertainty is first quantified through a fully parallelized predictive resampling scheme driven by model score functions, naturally accommodating modern differentiable density estimators such as normalizing flows. Posterior samples of the clustering are then obtained by applying density-based clustering to each random density sampled from the martingale posterior, enabling inference on any clustering-related quantity. Casting the estimand as a density functional also enables a rigorous frequentist convergence analysis. We illustrate the method through applications to image and single-cell RNA sequencing data, where it recovers meaningful clustering structures, including the assignment of previously unseen data and biologically interpretable cell grouping, while running in minutes on a single GPU.

articles.title_original: Adaptive Dual-Teacher Distillation with Subnetwork Rectification for Bridging Semantic Gaps in Black-Box Domain Adaptation
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2603.22908v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Assuming that neither source data nor source model parameters are accessible, black-box domain adaptation (BBDA) represents a highly practical yet challenging setting, where transferable knowledge is limited to the predictions of a black-box source model. Existing approaches exploit such knowledge via pseudo-label refinement or by leveraging vision-language models (ViLs), but they often fail to reconcile the inherent discrepancy between task-specific knowledge from black-box models and language-aligned semantic priors of ViLs, resulting in suboptimal integration and degraded adaptation performance. To address this challenge, we propose adaptive Dual-Teacher Distillation with Subnetwork Rectification (DDSR), a framework that explicitly reconciles these complementary yet inconsistent knowledge sources. DDSR employs an adaptive prediction fusion strategy to integrate predictions from the black-box source model and a ViL, generating reliable pseudo-labels for the target domain. A subnetwork-based regularization mechanism mitigates overfitting to noisy supervision by enforcing output consistency and gradient divergency. Furthermore, progressively improved target predictions iteratively refine both pseudo-labels and ViL prompts, enhancing semantic alignment. Finally, class-wise prototypes are used to further optimize target predictions via self-training. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that DDSR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, including those with access to source data or source model parameters.

articles.title_original: Abstract Compression of Conversational Audio Context for LLM-based ASR
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2603.26246v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Standard LLM-based speech recognition systems process utterances in isolation, limiting their ability to leverage conversational context. Here we study whether multimodal context from prior turns improves LLM-based ASR and how to represent that context efficiently. We find that, after supervised multi-turn training, conversational context mainly helps with the recognition of contextual entities. However, conditioning on raw context is expensive because the prior-turn audio embedding sequence grows rapidly with conversation length. To address this, we propose Abstract Compression, a learned latent abstraction of prior-turn audio that replaces each prior-turn audio sequence with a fixed number of latent tokens while retaining corresponding transcripts explicitly. On both in-domain and out-of-domain test sets, the compression-enabled model recovers part of the gains of raw-context conditioning with a smaller prior-turn audio footprint. We also provide targeted analyses of the compression setup and its tradeoffs.

articles.title_original: Simpler Logarithmic Approximation Algorithms for the Optimal Decision Tree and Adaptive Set Cover
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2604.12036v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study the problem of constructing a decision tree that identifies an unknown hypothesis from a given ground set, under both average- and worst-case cost. The Optimal Decision Tree (ODT) problem has been extensively studied in the literature, and $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$-approximation guarantees are known for each criterion, including a simultaneous guarantee for both (here $n$ is the number of hypotheses) [ICML]. Although most of the existing algorithm use simple greedy strategies, their analyses rely on intricate arguments. Since ODT is a fundamental problem with wide-ranging applications, we are interested in developing algorithms that are both effective and easy to understand.
  We present a new greedy algorithm with a simplified analysis that simultaneously achieves approximation factors below $3.65\log_2 n$ for worst-case cost and $7.3\log_2 n$ for average-case cost. Our algorithm for the Optimal Decision Tree behaves greedily with respect to the hereby introduced Separating Subfamily problem which asks for the cheapest subfamily of tests which partitions the hypotheses into pieces of small enough size. We show that the Separating Subfamily can itself be reduced to an instance of the well-known Maximum Coverage problem. At the core of our approach lies exploiting properties of cutting a clique into small pieces, where edges represent pairs of hypotheses to be separated. In the spirit of simplicity, we also provide a new and straightforward application of ODT: an $\mathcal{O}(\log (k\cdot n))$-approximation for the Adaptive Set Cover problem, where $k$ is the number of possible realizations.

articles.title_original: Non-Stationarity Breaks Permutation Surrogates in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: Diagnosis and Remedies
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2604.23716v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Reporting guidance for information-theoretic measures is rarely tested against ground truth. We test one guardrail in two multi-agent reinforcement learning games, a social dilemma and a coordination race, where directed influence between selected agent pairs is zero by construction, over 100 seeds. Omitting one precondition, exclusion of the non-stationary training transient, gives false-positive rates of 100.00% and 99.95%: agents annealing exploration independently, in runs that never met, are flagged as influencing one another. Excluding the transient reaches 3.05% in the social dilemma but 11.8% in the coordination game, so the non-stationarity must be treated and exclusion is neither the only way nor sufficient. What we recommend instead changes the null model. Series, statistic and estimand are left untouched: permuting the source within blocks of training time reaches 5.25% and 5.50%, the only one of the three at or below the size of the test in both games. The construction is not new, being a restricted permutation local to blocks of training time; the measurement is. A third null control, four learners in the social dilemma, defeats all three, and there conditioning costs three times what ours does, 15.20 points against 4.55. Titrating injected links separates it from conditioning on identical pairs, 82.5% against 58.0%, while the ablated test reports a positive with or without a link, so its apparent sensitivity is uninformative. Five block counts spanning 16 to 256 land in the nominal region. Code and data are released.

articles.title_original: RAM-H1200: A Unified Evaluation and Dataset on Hand Radiographs for Rheumatoid Arthritis
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.05616v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) assessment from hand radiographs requires multi-level analysis and modeling of anatomical structures and fine-grained local pathological changes. However, existing public resources do not support such unified multi-level analysis, often lacking full-hand coverage, fine-grained annotations, and consistent integration with clinical scoring systems. In particular, annotations that enable quantitative analysis of bone erosion (BE) remain scarce. RAM-H1200 contains 1,200 hand radiographs collected from six medical centers, with multi-level annotations including (i) whole-hand bone structure instance segmentation, (ii) pixel-level BE masks, (iii) SvdH-defined joint regions of interest, and (iv) joint-level SvdH scores for both BE and joint space narrowing (JSN). It is designed to evaluate whether models can jointly capture anatomical structure, localized erosive pathology, and clinically standardized RA severity from hand radiographs. The proposed BE masks enable, for the first time, quantitative BE analysis beyond coarse categorical grading by providing explicit spatial supervision for lesion extent and morphology. To our knowledge, RAM-H1200 is the first public large-scale benchmark that jointly supports whole-hand bone structure instance segmentation, pixel-level BE delineation, and clinically grounded joint-level SvdH scoring for both BE and JSN. Results across benchmark tasks show that anatomical modeling is substantially more mature than quantitative BE analysis: whole-hand bone segmentation achieves strong performance, whereas BE segmentation remains a major open challenge. By unifying anatomical structure modeling, quantitative lesion analysis, and clinically grounded SvdH scoring, RAM-H1200 provides a single benchmark for comprehensive RA analysis on hand radiographs.

articles.title_original: Dynamic Cross-Modal Prompt Generation for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.10765v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance through instruction tuning, yet real-world deployment often requires continual capability expansion across sequential tasks. In such scenarios, Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT) aims to acquire new capabilities while limiting catastrophic forgetting. Existing methods mainly follow a module-composition paradigm: they maintain task-level prompts or LoRA experts and dynamically route or aggregate a subset of them at inference. However, samples within the same task can still differ substantially in visual scenes, question intents, and reasoning demands. This motivates instance-level adaptation to individual query-image pairs rather than only selecting or combining task-level modules. To this end, we propose DRAPE (Dynamic Cross-Modal Prompt Generation), a prompt-learning framework that synthesizes continuous instance-specific soft prompts for MCIT. Instead of selecting prompts from a fixed pool, DRAPE derives prompt queries from the textual instruction and cross-attends to visual patch features, producing prompts conditioned on query-image pairs that are prepended to the frozen LLM. To mitigate forgetting during sequential updates, DRAPE applies null-space gradient projection to the shared projector and uses CLIP-based prototype routing for task-label-free generator selection at inference. Extensive experiments on MCIT benchmarks show that DRAPE achieves state-of-the-art performance among representative prompt-based and LoRA-based continual-learning baselines. Code is available at: https://github.com/LAMDA-CL/NeurIPS2026-Drape.

articles.title_original: StippleDiffusion: Capacity-Constrained Stippling using Controlled Diffusion
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.15816v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Stipple patterns, point sets whose local density tracks a target image, are traditionally produced by per-density iterative optimizers, which are slow, non-differentiable, and must be re-run from scratch for each new target. Learned alternatives have so far addressed only unconditional point generation; capacity-constrained, image-conditioned stippling has remained out of reach. We present the first diffusion-based sampler that simultaneously satisfies a learned local point-distribution prior and a continuous, image-defined capacity constraint at inference. The method is a ControlNet branch built on top of an optimal-transport-grid point-set diffusion baseline, conditioned on the target density map and a high-resolution image. Two design choices make the combination tractable: training and inference are restricted to the late-stage denoising regime, initialized from a density-weighted rejection sample, and the standard zero-convolution injection is replaced with a sigmoid-gated 1x1 projection that preserves the base model's blue-noise structure under hard density signals. A single trained checkpoint accepts arbitrary target densities at inference, generalizes to point budgets that were not seen during training, and produces stipples in time nearly independent of the output point count. On the Icons-50 benchmark, our learned sampler reaches parity with per-density-optimized baselines on every reported metric while remaining differentiable end-to-end.

articles.title_original: PACE: Geometry-Aware Bridge Transport for Single-Cell Trajectory Inference
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.18587v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Single-cell trajectory inference from destructive time-course snapshots is fundamentally ill-posed: neither cross-time cell correspondences nor continuous trajectories are observed, so the snapshot distributions alone do not uniquely determine the underlying dynamics. Existing optimal transport and flow-based methods typically couple cells by Euclidean proximity at observed clock times, which can misalign trajectories when development is asynchronous and cells sampled at the same experimental time occupy different latent pseudotime stages. We propose PACE, a trajectory inference framework that recovers geometry-consistent continuous transport dynamics from destructive time-course snapshots through three coupled components. First, PACE constructs a state- and time-dependent anisotropic Riemannian metric that assigns low transport cost along locally supported tangent directions while penalizing normal velocity components. Second, it alternates between refining cross-time couplings under the induced path-action cost and fitting endpoint-preserving neural bridges between adjacent snapshots. Third, it distills the learned bridge dynamics into a global continuous-time velocity field over cellular states. Across seven controlled and biological datasets covering nine held-out reconstruction experiments, PACE achieves the strongest overall reconstruction performance, reducing MMD, Wasserstein-1 distance, and Wasserstein-2 distance by 23.7% on average relative to the strongest competing baseline. PACE also improves RNA-velocity alignment by 15.4% on an embryoid body differentiation benchmark, without requiring explicit cell pairing, lineage tracing, or RNA-velocity supervision during training. Code is available at https://github.com/AI4Science-WestlakeU/PACE.

articles.title_original: QML-PipeGuard: Detecting Channel-Substitution Attacks on Quantum Machine Learning Pipelines in Untrusted Clouds
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.25066v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: As machine-learning workloads move onto quantum hardware they inherit a trust problem classical AI deployments have largely solved and quantum ones have not: quantum machine learning (QML) is already sold as a cloud service, and a customer cannot check that the circuit they paid for is actually the circuit that ran. We show the gap is exploitable. A malicious or cost-cutting provider can substitute the declared quantum channel with one that reproduces every accuracy test the customer performs, passes the single-observable checks used in practice, and still differs from the declared computation at the channel level. We call this a channel-substitution attack and instantiate it in three deployments: audit evasion, service downgrade, and result forgery in reproducibility review. QML-PipeGuard detects the attack at runtime from measurement statistics the customer already collects. Its guarantee is two-sided, stated in the distance a local verifier measures: any substitution shifting a single-qubit output marginal by $\delta$ in trace norm forces a contract deviation of at least $\delta/\sqrt{3}$, the constant tight and independent of qubit count; the guarantee is relative to the chosen observable family and reference-input set. For local-unitary substitutions the adversary's blind set is characterised exactly, as a commutation condition, which gives the defender a rule for choosing challenge inputs that shrinks it. A finite-shot budget rule bounds false accepts and false alarms at once, one tolerance separates attack from the benign drift observed here, and every decision enters a hash-anchored audit trail. On an IBM Heron r2 processor a substituted quantum-kernel intrusion-detection pipeline evades the weak contract and our verifier halts it, while the honest channel stays within tolerance.

articles.title_original: Beyond a Single Direction: Chain-of-Thought Disrupts Simple Steering of Refusal
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.26772v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) generate chain-of-thought (CoT) traces before producing final outputs, introducing a dynamic internal state that may complicate control mechanisms such as refusal. Unlike instruction-tuned LLMs, where refusal is mediated by a single directional subspace, refusal in large reasoning models (LRMs) additionally depends on the CoT. In DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B, activation steering reverses refusal in only 39% of cases when the CoT is kept fixed, but removing the CoT entirely increases this to 70%, indicating that the CoT actively reinforces refusal. In a two-stage intervention where the model regenerates its CoT under activation steering, refusal is reversed in 94% of cases, while the resulting CoT alone retains 48% of this effect even after steering is removed. This suggests that the CoT can carry and reconstruct the compliance signal independently. These findings indicate that refusal in LRMs is jointly encoded in residual stream activations and CoT. This joint activation makes LRM more robust against activation-level interventions alone, but exposes CoT to a possible alternative surface attack.

articles.title_original: The Shape of Wisdom: How Language Models Converge on an Answer
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2606.01202v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: When a language model answers a factual question, where does its internal state go? We asked four open models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Llama-3.2-1B) 2,256 factual questions whose answers recur, such as the country a person is a citizen of. At every layer, we recorded the state from which the answer is produced. Questions that receive the same answer converge on a shared region of state space, which we summarise by its centre, the answer centroid. The answer becomes readable within a single layer. In every model, the share of questions whose state lies nearest its own answer's centroid jumps at one layer, between 47% and 71% of the way through the network. The centroids follow the answer the model gives rather than the question: the centroid of a country learned from questions about people's citizenship also identifies that country in questions about towns and films. The model also uses the centroids. After the jump, moving the state of a wrongly answered question to the right answer's centroid makes the model give the right answer in 83%-97% of cases late in the network, against 2%-4% for a random move of the same size. Before the jump, moves of the same size almost never work. Near misses, in which the model answers wrongly but picks the right option in multiple choice, can be seen from the onset layer, where the right answer's centroid is already among the nearest to the state. This signal is about as informative as the right answer's rank in the model's final output, and more informative than the model's confidence in its reply.

articles.title_original: Decomposing Refusal Steering in Mixture-of-Experts Models
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2606.04160v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Safety alignment in instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) depends on a model's ability to reliably refuse harmful or disallowed requests. Recent work has shown that a steering vector can be applied to a dense LLM during inference to suppress refusal behavior and induce responses to harmful requests. We extend this refusal steering method to three open-source Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs to decompose and better understand how refusal mechanisms operate across MoE components. We find that steering performance is uninhibited by the complex routing patterns inherent to the MoE architecture, and that a single expert recovers 78% of the full steering effect on average when free to select its own location. However, expert-level steering only recovers 54% on average when constrained to the location used by full-layer steering, a gap that widens further under safety-related system prompts. Our results also show that refusal signals captured by these steering methods differ from those captured by expert routing behavior. Together, these results suggest that refusal behavior is distributed unevenly across the MoE LLM architecture rather than governed by a single unified mechanism.

articles.title_original: Service-Induced Congestion in Memory-Constrained LLM Serving
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2606.15555v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In large language model (LLM) serving, each request accumulates persistent graphics processing unit (GPU) memory during service as its key-value cache grows with every generated token. Under high concurrency, aggregate memory usage therefore increases endogenously over time: the service process itself creates future capacity pressure. When memory capacity is exceeded, systems evict active requests, discarding cached state and restarting them later, which wastes computation and reduces throughput. We develop a discrete-time dynamical model of memory-constrained LLM inference that captures admission, memory growth, and eviction under continuous batching. In the saturated-input regime, the system admits both eviction-free fixed points and limit cycles with evictions. For homogeneous workloads, we show that the eviction-free equilibrium is unstable and that, except for a Lebesgue-measure-zero exact-capture set, the system converges to a unique worst-case limit cycle that is asymptotically stable outside this exceptional set, with throughput losses as large as 50%. For heterogeneous workloads, we prove a stability criterion in the two-class common-input setting and explain how the survival-polynomial mechanism generalizes to multiple classes and heterogeneous-input lengths. Under an input-dominated scaling regime, coprime decoding lengths stabilize the eviction-free equilibrium, while non-coprime lengths create synchronized modes that drive instability. These results characterize when workload heterogeneity desynchronizes completions and helps stabilize memory-constrained serving. More broadly, we identify service-induced congestion as a structural instability mechanism and derive scheduling design principles for sustaining high throughput.

articles.title_original: Probe, Don't Prompt: A Hidden-State Probe for Metadata Filtering in Multi-Meta-RAG
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2607.03929v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Multi-Meta-RAG improves retrieval for multi-hop question answering by filtering a vector store on metadata, specifically the news source and the publication date, which it extracts from each query using GPT-3.5. This extractor requires a proprietary API call for every query, and its output is not restricted to the allowed sources: even though the prompt specifies 49 sources, GPT-3.5 generates 128 distinct source names, 79 of which do not appear on the list. We show that the source part of this extractor can be replaced by a local, deterministic probe trained on the hidden states of a small open-source language model. The probe is a multi-label logistic classifier on the mean-pooled hidden states of one layer, trained with a class-balanced loss on the gold evidence sources. Using 5-fold cross-validation to select the layer, we evaluate four models ranging from 135M to 1.5B parameters out-of-fold across all 2556 MultiHop-RAG queries. The probe reaches a set-exact accuracy of 90.9%, compared to 88.0% for a substring baseline and 80.9% for GPT-3.5. The difference comes from null queries, for which GPT-3.5 never predicts an empty source set. Across the remaining queries, all three methods achieve set-exact accuracies within 1.1 percentage points of each other. Unlike earlier probing work, we use the probe as a component of a retrieval pipeline rather than for interpretation. For all four models, the cross-validation selects one of the first layers, in contrast to the middle layers reported for retrieval tasks. We attribute this to the source name appearing verbatim in 95.4% of gold query-source pairs. The 135M model is 1.5 percentage points less accurate than the 1.5B model, so the filter requires only a partial forward pass through a small model and one linear layer. The code is available at https://github.com/mxpoliakov/Multi-Meta-RAG.

articles.title_original: $H^2(\Omega)$ A Priori Error Bounds for Boundary-Adapted PINNs Solving Elliptic Dirichlet Problems
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2607.19167v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study the numerical resolution of uniformly elliptic Dirichlet boundary value problems (BVPs) by minimization of the PDE residual over a hypothesis space of Neural Networks made to satisfy exactly the boundary conditions through multiplication by a user-defined \emph{distance-to-boundary approximation} $\rho$. While an $L^2(\partial\Omega)$ boundary penalty cannot generally guarantee $H^2(\Omega)$ error control, we show that exact enforcement can, provided $\rho$ is chosen appropriately. More precisely, we identify a sharp sufficient condition on $\rho$ preserving the regularity needed for $H^2(\Omega)$ error control, provide practical constructions of such $\rho$ for general smooth domains $\Omega$, and refer to the resulting networks as \emph{boundary-adapted}. For boundary-adapted Rectified Quadratic Unit (ReQU) and hyperbolic tangent (tanh) networks, we then derive explicit high-probability $H^2(\Omega)$ convergence rates by combining approximation-theoretic and statistical-learning arguments, making explicit the dependence on $\rho$. Numerical experiments support our theoretical results, showing that appropriate choices of $\rho$ improve accuracy and convergence, while poorly chosen distance functions can substantially degrade the solution. Our proof also yields new VC-dimension bounds for hypothesis spaces of higher-order derivatives of ReQU and tanh networks, together with new approximation bounds for shallow ReQU networks in higher-order Sobolev norms, all of which are of important independent interest.

articles.title_original: CFR without Unbiasedness: Debit-Budgeted Public Feedback
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2608.14761v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: At a finite public-chance cut, partial counterfactual regret minimization (CFR) can evaluate successive outcome batches at learner states changed by earlier batches. Balanced coverage then lacks the conditional unbiasedness used by Monte Carlo CFR analyses. We introduce \emph{target debit}, the one-sided cumulative underestimation needed to transfer regret on delivered feedback to the dense target game. Our central theorem bounds weighted exploitability by delivered-row regret, target debit, and a native alternating-update correction. This yields Debit-Budgeted CFR (DB-CFR), which selects a public plan from completed history, executes it once, and settles its debit afterward. Complete coverage has zero debit and supplies exact recovery. With at most $\ell$ unsettled blocks, hidden debit is bounded by the sum of the $\ell$ largest predictable block envelopes; for fixed $\ell$ and polynomial output weights, the resulting $O(T^{-1})$ term preserves the additive-RM/RM+ rate. A finite converse gives equal-metadata plans with charges $0$ and $11/8$, proving that a nontrivial strict-budget decision requires semantic information or bounded post-execution settlement. In two released heads-up no-limit hold'em turn endgames, all 42 registered shallow comparisons favor partial coverage before complete coverage overtakes it between 32 and 64 rounds. In public Leduc, a lagged rule fixed on four development orders beats the best matched-recurrence-work fixed width on all ten unseen orders (median NashConv gain $0.0456$) without future candidate replay.
